titre: Fed's Hammack questions whether Fed policy is tight enough as inflation risks build
titre_fr: Fed's Hammack questions whether Fed policy is tight enough as inflation risks build
contenu:
The remarks lean hawkish and add to the case for further Fed tightening, a backdrop that tends to support the dollar and push short-dated Treasury yields higher. Her view that financial conditions are not restrictive is the more market-relevant line, because it argues against any assumption that the September hike was enough. Fuel costs remain central to the input cost pressures firms are reporting, so oil prices are the variable most likely to shape whether her expectations worry materialises. A firmer rate path is also a headwind for gold, which has tended to fall as hike expectations rise.

---

Still to come:

---

Hammack is less worried about where inflation is today than about Americans starting to expect it, and that distinction could lower her bar for backing another hike.

Summary:

Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack warned on Thursday that a deterioration in the public’s inflation expectations would likely require a more forceful response from the central bank. Her remarks add to signs that policymakers are prepared to keep tightening.

Speaking at an event hosted by Goldman Sachs in New York, Hammack said her main concern was the emergence of an inflationary mindset, in which households and businesses come to expect persistent price pressures. If that took hold, she said, it would become much harder for monetary policy to do its job, and the Fed might need to move further than it otherwise would.

Hammack said businesses were reporting substantial pressure from input costs, and that she was hearing more from lower-income Americans who are struggling with inflation. She stressed the value of anecdotal reports from businesses and communities as a guide to the economy, alongside official data.

On the policy stance, Hammack said it is difficult to pin down where the neutral interest rate lies, the level that neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. She added that financial conditions do not currently appear restrictive. That view implies current settings may not be doing enough to bring inflation down.

Her comments come with the Fed already on a hiking path. The central bank raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4.00% in September, its first increase in this cycle, and policymakers next meet on 27 and 28 October. Hammack votes on policy this year.

Taken together, the remarks point to a preference for further tightening rather than any pause. Her emphasis on expectations, rather than the current inflation rate alone, matters. It suggests her threshold for supporting another hike could be lower if surveys or business reports show price pressures becoming entrenched. At the same time, she did not commit to the timing of any move.

The comments are likely to reinforce market attention on Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who speaks later in the Asian session, and on upcoming measures of inflation expectations.

titre: Warsh speaks in Bangkok after hot CPI: is a second Fed hike coming in October?
titre_fr: Warsh speaks in Bangkok after hot CPI: is a second Fed hike coming in October?
contenu:
This is the highest-impact appearance of the day. Short-dated Treasuries and the dollar are most exposed to any signal that October is live, after Wednesday’s inflation data lifted two-year yields sharply. Oil is the central variable: fuel costs tied to the Iran war are the main source of the latest inflation jump, so a sustained move in crude feeds directly into Fed hike expectations. A hawkish Warsh would likely add pressure on equities and gold, which slid after the CPI release as yields rose. A guarded performance, sticking to his dislike of forward guidance, would leave the hike debate resting on data.

---

Warsh is the big one today! But not the only one:

---

Warsh has spent two months arguing inflation will not fix itself, and a hot September CPI hands him the evidence just as markets debate whether the Fed’s second hike comes in October or December.

Summary:

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh appears in a moderated conversation at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday, days after US inflation data strengthened the case for further tightening. The session is scheduled for 03:30 GMT (23:30 US Eastern on Thursday), less than two weeks before the Federal Open Market Committee meets on 27 and 28 October.

The Fed is on a hiking path. In September it raised the federal funds target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4.00%, its first increase since 2023, according to the Fed’s published statement. The vote was unanimous. The move reversed the last of three quarter-point cuts delivered in late 2025 and signalled a clear shift in priorities towards inflation.

That shift was driven by prices. Inflation has run above the Fed’s 2% goal for years, and higher fuel costs linked to the Iran war have pushed it further from target. September consumer price data released on Wednesday showed headline inflation rising again and beating forecasts, with core inflation also edging higher. The Fed said in September that inflation remains elevated and that its decision would support a timelier return to target.

The labour market, the other half of the Fed’s dual mandate, is less of a constraint for now. Hiring has slowed markedly in recent months and earlier figures have been revised lower. However, the unemployment rate has stayed within a narrow range and remains low by historical standards.

Warsh has made his priorities clear. In his Jackson Hole speech in August he said inflation was too high and would not return to target on its own, arguing that underlying price pressures had not meaningfully improved. He judged inflation a bigger concern than the jobs market. He also said current rates were not restricting activity given strong investment and consumer spending, and described short-term rates as the Fed’s main tool against inflation. He has also said he opposes giving forward guidance on future meetings.

Other officials have leaned the same way. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack is a voter this year and dissented in favour of a hike in July. She said this week she believes rates need to rise further to restrain demand, while keeping an open mind on the timing.

Markets had leaned towards a hold in October after a weak September jobs report. Wednesday’s inflation data pushed Treasury yields higher as traders added to bets on further tightening. In September, most Fed officials projected at least one more increase by year-end.

Several things are worth watching:

titre: Macklem in Bangkok: oil, tariffs and job losses test the Bank of Canada’s hike case
titre_fr: Macklem in Bangkok: oil, tariffs and job losses test the Bank of Canada’s hike case
contenu:
The Canadian dollar and short-dated Canada yields are most exposed if Macklem is drawn on policy. With October hike odds already slashed after the jobs data, any hawkish signal would carry more surprise value than a cautious one. Oil cuts both ways for Canada: higher crude supports the terms of trade and the currency, but it is also the main source of above-target inflation, so a sustained move in prices would shift both the inflation debate and the loonie. Tariff headlines remain a second source of volatility.

---

Earlier:

---

Macklem has argued the Bank can look through an oil shock only until it spreads, and two months of job losses have made markets doubt the spreading starts soon enough to justify an October hike.

Summary:

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem joins a panel on artificial intelligence and the global economy at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok on Friday. It comes less than two weeks before the central bank’s 28 October rate decision. The session is scheduled for 04:15 GMT (00:15 US Eastern), according to the Bank’s media advisory. The topic is AI rather than monetary policy, so any comments on rates would most likely come in response to questions.

The policy rate stands at 2.25%, where it has been since a quarter-point cut in October last year, according to the Bank of Canada. Governing Council has held at every decision since. The most recent hold was on 2 September, when it said it was prepared to adjust policy as needed.

Headline inflation is running above the 2% target, pushed up by higher gasoline prices linked to the Middle East conflict and damaged refining capacity. Core measures, however, have stayed close to target, and the Bank has said it sees little sign so far of energy costs spreading into wider prices. In a speech last month, Macklem said the Bank can look through the direct effect of higher oil, but only while those pressures stay contained. He added that it does not want to be too slow to respond if they broaden.

The growth picture complicates the decision. The economy rebounded strongly in the second quarter. However, new US tariffs following the breakdown of Canada-US trade talks have clouded the outlook, and Macklem has warned growth could slow sharply late this year if they persist.

The labour market has also turned. Canada shed jobs in both August and September, and the unemployment rate rose back to where it started the year. That points to continued slack in the economy.

The jobs data shifted expectations. Markets scaled back the odds of an October hike to well below even after the September report, while still leaning towards a move by December. Some economists now expect the Bank to hold this month, though others had been forecasting an increase.

Three questions matter if Macklem is drawn on policy:

titre: Preview: Nagel and Klingbeil in Bangkok: three themes as the ECB weighs a December hike
titre_fr: Preview: Nagel and Klingbeil in Bangkok: three themes as the ECB weighs a December hike
contenu:
The euro and short-dated Bunds are most sensitive to any steer from Nagel on December. A clear endorsement of a further hike would firm rate support for the single currency. Any nod to French fiscal strain as a reason for caution would point the other way. Oil remains the key driver of the ECB debate: Nagel has called it one of the indicators the Governing Council must now watch, so a sustained easing in crude and gas prices would weaken the case for more tightening. Klingbeil’s comments on German spending matter for Bund supply and longer-dated yields.

---

It's a huge session for central bank speakers today:

---

Nagel is in Bangkok as one of the ECB’s firmer voices on tightening, but questions on French debt could test how far he is willing to push.

Summary:

Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel holds a joint press conference with German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in Bangkok on Friday, on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank annual meetings. It comes less than two weeks before the European Central Bank’s 29 October policy decision. The briefing is scheduled for 02:30 GMT (22:30 US Eastern on Thursday).

The ECB has been on a tightening path since the Iran war pushed energy costs higher. It raised its deposit rate by a quarter point in June and again in September, taking it to 2.50%, according to the ECB’s published key rates. Before that, the rate had been held at 2% for a year.

Euro area inflation is running well above the 2% target and climbed further in September, driven mainly by energy. The ECB’s own September projections show inflation staying above target well into next year, with underlying price pressures still building into early 2027. The labour market has held steady, and wage growth has so far shown little response to the energy shock.

Nagel is one of the Governing Council’s more hawkish voices. He said in late September that rates sit around neutral, but that a move into mildly restrictive territory could not be ruled out if price pressures persist. He has since argued that high uncertainty calls for flexibility rather than inaction, flagging low European gas storage as a particular vulnerability.

Germany offers a brighter backdrop than it has for some time. Nagel has described a gradual recovery supported by foreign orders and public spending on infrastructure and defence. Berlin this month sharply raised its growth forecast for this year.

Markets and most economists expect the ECB to hold in October before a further hike in December. Citigroup has argued that French fiscal strain could make December the last move. French bond spreads over Germany widened earlier this month to their highest in well over a decade.

Three themes are likely to dominate the briefing:

titre: BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor
titre_fr: BOE, Bailey, Bangkok. What could possibly go wrong? Preview and 3 questions for the Governor
contenu:
Sterling and short-dated gilts are most exposed to Bailey’s remarks, because front-end pricing already assumes a November hike is close to a done deal. If he endorses that view, rate support for the pound stays in place. Any hint of patience, or emphasis on the softer jobs market, could pull hike odds lower and weigh on the currency. Oil remains the swing factor: the Bank’s case for tightening rests on oil and gas prices staying well above pre-war levels, so any easing in Brent would weaken the hawkish argument more than anything Bailey says.

---

Bailey has spent a month telling markets that high energy prices are making a hold harder to justify, and Bangkok is his chance to confirm or cool a November hike they have almost fully priced.

Summary:

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey takes the stage at the Institute of International Finance’s annual membership meeting in Bangkok, held alongside the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, on Friday, with financial markets increasingly convinced that the Bank’s next move will be a rate rise. Bailey is due to appear in conversation with IIF President and Chief Executive Tim Adams at 02:00 GMT (22:00 US Eastern on Thursday), less than three weeks before the Monetary Policy Committee’s 5 November decision.

Bank Rate stands at 3.75%, where it has been since a narrow 5-4 vote delivered a quarter-point cut last December. At its most recent meeting in September, the MPC held the rate by a 6-3 majority, according to the Bank’s published minutes. Bailey was among the six voting to hold, and the other three preferred an immediate increase to 4%.

Inflation is the central problem. Consumer price inflation is running well above the 2% target, as it has for almost all of the past five years. The Bank expects it to climb further into early next year as higher oil, gas and electricity costs linked to the Iran war work through to household bills. The Bank has said those costs have so far had only a limited effect on wider wage and price setting. It has also said that the longer energy prices stay high, the more likely it becomes that Bank Rate will need to rise.

The jobs market offers a partial counterweight. Unemployment has drifted higher and private-sector pay growth has eased, and the slack that implies is a key reason the majority preferred to wait in September.

Bailey’s tone has hardened since that vote. He warned in late September that persistently high energy prices would make it harder to keep rates on hold, adding that the Bank could not wait for complete evidence on inflation expectations. He has since argued that looking through an energy shock only works while expectations stay anchored. Markets have taken the hint: traders price a high probability of a November hike, and a Reuters poll this week found a large majority of economists expect Bank Rate to rise to 4%.

Three questions will shape the reaction:

titre: RBNZ’s Conway says October rate decision completely open, OCR more likely to rise
titre_fr: RBNZ’s Conway says October rate decision completely open, OCR more likely to rise
contenu:
Conway’s comments keep a late-October hike live, which should support the New Zealand dollar against currencies where rate expectations are falling, most notably the Australian dollar after Thursday’s weak jobs report. That divergence makes AUD/NZD a natural expression of the gap between a dovish-leaning RBA and a still-hawkish RBNZ. By declining to commit, the RBNZ leaves markets highly sensitive to the next round of New Zealand data, so expect pricing to swing between a hold and a hike before the decision. A firm tightening bias also limits the scope for New Zealand yields to fall much further in the near term.

-The RBNZ wants the market to know a hike is coming, just not necessarily when.

Summary:

The Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s next interest rate decision in late October is “completely open”, chief economist Paul Conway said, while repeating that the central bank still sees the official cash rate as more likely to rise than fall.

Speaking on the sidelines of the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Conway said the bank wants to keep its options open between holding the rate steady and raising it by 25 basis points. The RBNZ continues to see the next move in the OCR as most likely to be higher, he said, but it has not decided on timing.

Conway said recent moves in oil prices and the New Zealand dollar have added to inflation pressure in the short term. Even so, the bank remains confident that inflation will slow back into its 1% to 3% target band next year.

The comments leave the October decision finely balanced. By describing the meeting as completely open, Conway avoided pre-committing the bank to a hike, while his reaffirmation of a tightening bias makes clear that a cut is not on the table. That gives the RBNZ room to respond to incoming data, including inflation figures, before the announcement.

The RBNZ’s stance stands out against shifts elsewhere in the region. Across the Tasman, softer Australian jobs data on Thursday prompted traders to cut the odds of a November Reserve Bank of Australia hike to around 15%. In the United States, a hotter inflation report has pushed markets to price a strong chance of a Federal Reserve hike in December.

The key question for the late-October meeting is whether short-term price pressures from energy and the currency prove strong enough to justify acting now, or whether the bank’s confidence in inflation returning to target next year allows it to wait a little longer.

titre: ECB’s Santos Pereira says euro zone inflation is not spreading beyond energy
titre_fr: ECB’s Santos Pereira says euro zone inflation is not spreading beyond energy
contenu:
The comments support the view that the ECB can hold its nerve on an energy-led price shock, which should limit pressure for tighter policy in the near term and leave the euro without a fresh rate-driven boost. His attribution of higher yields to fiscal issues rather than inflation is notable for bond traders, since it suggests the ECB sees the selloff as a matter for governments rather than for monetary policy. That points to limited appetite to lean against yields through policy. Natural gas is the swing factor, and a cold start to winter would quickly test his relaxed stance and could revive hawkish pricing.

Álvaro Santos Pereira is the governor of the Banco de Portugal, Portugal’s central bank. That makes him a member of the ECB’s Governing Council.

The ECB can live with an energy shock as long as it stays an energy shock, and so far, says Santos Pereira, it has.

Summary:

Energy-driven inflation in the euro zone is not spreading to the wider economy, European Central Bank policymaker Alvaro Santos Pereira said, offering a reassuring signal for the bank as it weighs the risk of higher prices.

Speaking at the Bangkok Economic Festival, the Portuguese central bank governor said the good news was that inflation in Europe had not broadened so far. He pointed to the share of goods and services with prices rising by more than 3% or 4%, which he said had stayed broadly stable over roughly the past two years.

Santos Pereira also made clear where the line sits. If inflation does start to broaden, he said, central banks will be forced to act. That suggests the ECB is prepared to look through an energy shock for now, but would respond if price increases began to spread into other categories.

He flagged natural gas as the main risk. A winter like last year’s would create a problem for gas prices, he said, which would feed directly into energy costs for households and businesses. He also said the recent rise in bond yields was more closely tied to fiscal concerns than to the inflation outlook.

The measure he cited is a breadth or diffusion gauge, which tracks how widespread price increases are rather than how fast prices are rising on average. It is gaining attention among central bankers. Bloomberg Economics highlighted a similar measure for the United States this week, showing fewer US consumer price categories running hot in September. Bank of Japan board member Junko Koeda pointed to the more than 70% of Japanese CPI items rising year on year as evidence that inflation there is taking hold.

For the ECB, the readings to watch are the next euro zone inflation figures, the path of natural gas prices as winter approaches, and whether the share of fast-rising prices starts to climb.

titre: AUD lower: Australian jobs fall 39,300 in September, unemployment at five-year high of 4.7%
titre_fr: AUD lower: Australian jobs fall 39,300 in September, unemployment at five-year high of 4.7%
contenu:
The report shifts the RBA debate from when the next hike comes to whether it comes at all, with a pause now looking the likelier near-term outcome. That leaves the Australian dollar out of step with the wider market. While gold and major currencies have risen against the US dollar on lower Treasury yields, the Aussie has stayed near its post-data lows, as a narrowing rate outlook at home offsets the broader dollar weakness. Further AUD underperformance is likely on crosses such as AUD/NZD and AUD/JPY if markets keep paring RBA hike bets. The noisy nature of the data means the next release, and the RBA’s revised forecasts in November, will carry extra weight.

--Australia’s jobs market blinked in September, and with it went most of the market’s appetite for a November RBA hike.

Summary:

Australian employment unexpectedly fell in September, while the unemployment rate held at a five-year high of 4.7%, prompting traders to scale back bets on another Reserve Bank of Australia rate hike.

Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Thursday showed employment dropped by 39,300 in the month, well short of forecasts for a gain of around 20,000. August’s increase was revised down to 29,300. The decline was driven entirely by part-time work, which slumped by 73,700, its weakest month in five years, while full-time employment rose by 34,400.

The unemployment rate was steady at 4.7%, above expectations of 4.6%. August’s rate was revised up to 4.7% from 4.6%, although only just: unrounded, the jobless rate was 4.72% in September against 4.65% in August. A sharp drop in the participation rate to 66.8% from 67.1%, below the 67.0% expected, limited the rise in unemployment, as fewer people were looking for work. Hours worked rose 0.1% and underemployment edged up to 6.3%.

The ABS urged caution in interpreting the seasonally adjusted figures, citing ongoing volatility in the data. That volatility comes at an awkward time for the RBA, which relies on the labour figures to judge how tighter policy is affecting the economy. The split between full-time and part-time jobs, and the swing in participation, have both been noisy from month to month.

Even so, the trend is softening. The unemployment rate averaged 4.6% over the quarter, well above the RBA’s forecast, which is likely to force the bank to revise its projections higher at its November meeting. With the RBA operating under a dual mandate of price stability and full employment, a weaker jobs market makes the risks around further tightening more balanced.

Markets moved quickly to reflect that. Pricing for a November RBA rate hike fell and markets no longer favour a hike before the first half of 2027. Australian three-year government bond yields fell circa 10 basis points.

The Australian dollar dropped on the release and has stayed near its lows, standing out against gains in gold and other major currencies as US Treasury yields have fallen.

titre: BOJ’s Koeda says bank should not be overly cautious about raising rates
titre_fr: BOJ’s Koeda says bank should not be overly cautious about raising rates
contenu:
Koeda’s message leans hawkish: by placing the neutral rate considerably above the current 1.25% policy rate and warning against excessive caution, she keeps further BOJ hikes firmly on the table. That should offer the yen some support, particularly against a backdrop where Fed hike expectations have also risen, which narrows the room for the yen to weaken on rate differentials alone. Her observation that the yen has lost some of its safe-haven role is notable for currency traders, since it suggests geopolitical shocks may now hurt the yen through higher oil import costs rather than help it. Japanese government bond yields may also face upward pressure if markets price a faster path toward neutral.

-

Koeda’s message to markets is that 1.25% is not the destination, and the BOJ shouldn’t let caution slow the trip.

Summary:

Bank of Japan policy board member Junko Koeda said on Thursday that the central bank should not become overly cautious about raising interest rates, pointing to considerable upside risks to prices and financial conditions that remain accommodative.

In a speech to local leaders in Kumamoto, Koeda said the BOJ should adjust its policy rate in a timely manner while keeping in mind the estimated range of the neutral interest rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. She said the neutral rate is likely considerably above 1%, which she described as roughly the bottom of the estimated range, and that one estimate based on potential growth could put it above 2%. The BOJ’s own estimates imply a nominal neutral rate of around 1.1% to 2.5%. Following the BOJ’s rate hike in September, the overnight call rate stands at around 1.25%, leaving room for further increases on her reasoning.

Koeda said underlying inflation appears to be becoming anchored at around 2%, in line with the BOJ’s price stability target. More than 70% of the over 500 items in Japan’s consumer price index are rising year on year, and the distribution of price changes has shifted higher, she said. With wages also increasing steadily, sustained inflation appears to be taking hold more than before.

She highlighted several sources of upside risk to prices. Geopolitical shocks, including the situation in the Middle East since the spring, have repeatedly driven up crude oil and commodity prices. Koeda also noted that the yen has been less reliable as a safe haven in recent crises, continuing to weaken during this year’s Middle East escalation as oil surged, which has pushed up import costs. Strong global demand linked to artificial intelligence is adding further inflationary pressure.

On the economy, Koeda described recent indicators as solid overall, citing high corporate profits, moderate growth in business investment and continued wage gains. She said rising rates were not expected to significantly reduce household consumption, and that firms’ funding conditions remained favourable.

Koeda also stressed the need to keep normalising the BOJ’s balance sheet, saying its substantial size should not be underestimated. The BOJ is reducing its monthly government bond purchases in stages and plans to hold them at about 2 trillion yen a month from April 2027.

titre: ICYMI: Citi now expects a December Fed rate hike after hotter September US inflation
titre_fr: ICYMI: Citi now expects a December Fed rate hike after hotter September US inflation
contenu:
Citi’s shift removes one of the last prominent holdouts against a December hike, so the debate moves from whether the Fed tightens again to when. The swing in October pricing, which spiked after the data and then faded, shows traders are uncertain about the timing and are likely to react strongly to any Fed speaker who leans either way before the meeting. A higher-for-longer path, with cuts pushed out to mid-2027, tends to support the US dollar and Treasury yields and to weigh on rate-sensitive assets. The core detail matters most: inflation spreading beyond gasoline is harder for the Fed to look through than an energy spike alone.

--Thehot CPI printwas enough to turn Citi from a Fed sceptic into a December hiker, and markets are now asking whether October comes first.

Summary:

Citigroup now expects the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by 25 basis points in December, after US consumer inflation for September came in above expectations. The bank had previously forecast no further Fed moves this year, even though financial markets had already largely priced in a December increase.

Citi said it expects the Fed to leave rates unchanged after that December hike, and does not see cuts beginning until June 2027.

Wednesday’s Consumer Price Index report showed headline inflation rising to 3.7% in the year to September from 3.4% in August, slightly above the 3.6% expected. Prices rose 0.6% on the month, in line with forecasts, driven by a surge in gasoline costs. The more worrying detail for policymakers was that price pressures spread beyond energy. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, climbed to 2.6% from 2.4%, above the 2.5% expected, with a monthly gain of around 0.3% against forecasts of 0.2%. That raised concern that underlying inflation could prove sticky.

Markets reacted quickly. Rate futures pointed to roughly a 94% probability of a December hike. Pricing for the Fed’s October 27 to 28 meeting moved sharply too. CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed the implied chance of an October hike jumping to around 47% after the data, from roughly 22% beforehand. That has since eased, with FedWatch showing a probability of around 32% at the time of writing.

The shift leaves the October meeting as a genuine decision point rather than a formality. Markets are still treating a December move as close to certain, but the timing of the next hike has become a live debate.

Citi’s change of view matters because it brings one of the major Wall Street forecasters into line with market pricing. It also signals that a single inflation report showing broader price pressure can be enough to shift expectations. Attention now turns to remaining Fed commentary before the October meeting and to the next round of inflation data, including the September PCE figures, for confirmation of whether price pressures are spreading or easing.

titre: Fed’s Daly: more rate hikes likely needed, but no urgency to move in October
titre_fr: Fed’s Daly: more rate hikes likely needed, but no urgency to move in October
contenu:
Daly’s comments are the clearest pushback yet against the jump in October hike pricing that followed the CPI data. Expect them to trim the odds of a move on October 27-28 without denting expectations for a December increase. That mix would ease some pressure on the front end of the Treasury curve while leaving longer-dated yields anchored to a higher-for-longer outlook. Because Daly linked headline inflation directly to gasoline prices, oil remains the key swing factor. A further surge in crude tied to the Iran war would test her view that the Fed can afford to wait. Daly agrees the Fed probably has more hiking to do, but she sees no reason to rush it out the door this month.

Summary:

The Federal Reserve will probably need to raise interest rates further to bring down inflation, San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said on Wednesday, but she signalled there is no need to act at the central bank’s October 27-28 meeting. Daly made the remarks in an exclusive interview with Reuters.

Daly said further adjustments were more likely than not, but that she was still weighing their timing. She said she did not feel any urgency to decide on a limited set of information and believed the Fed had the time it needed. In her view, reacting when there is time to make a good decision would be imprudent, and it is better for policymakers to be thoughtful and deliberate.

Her comments came on the same day asSeptember consumer price data, which showed inflation running at 3.7% from a year earlier, above expectations and well over the Fed’s 2% goal. Daly said the figures showed gasoline prices driving headline inflation, while core inflation, which strips out volatile food and energy costs, remained sticky, as she had expected. She said it was not yet clear whether inflation would ease as recent shocks fade, or worsen if they persist.

Daly said the risks of inflation staying above target remain elevated. A stable labour market, she added, means the Fed can concentrate on price stability. She also said she found it reassuring that markets had calmed after an initially strong reaction to the CPI report, and that investors understood how the Fed would respond.

The remarks help define where policymakers stand ahead of this month’s meeting. Earlier on Wednesday, Chicago Fed President AustanGoolsbee called the CPI data discouraging, pointing to persistent services inflation. The Fed’sBeige Book survey showed price pressures intensifyingacross parts of the country, driven increasingly by diesel costs. The CPI release had lifted market expectations of an October hike, and Daly’s comments suggest she would prefer to wait.

The Fed raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4% in September and signalled one more increase this year. Most officials have pointed to December rather than October as the likelier timing, and Daly’s comments fit that view.

titre: Fed catch up - Goolsbee calls CPI discouraging as Beige Book flags diesel-fuelled price pressure
titre_fr: Fed catch up - Goolsbee calls CPI discouraging as Beige Book flags diesel-fuelled price pressure
contenu:
Together, the two releases make an October hike harder to dismiss. Markets are pricing close to a 40% chance of a move on October 27-28, even though key officials had steered expectations toward December. The oil link is central: diesel costs from the Iran war now run through freight, farming and airfares, which raises the risk of second-round effects the Fed cannot easily look through. That supports Treasury yields at the front end and the US dollar, and keeps mortgage rates under upward pressure. Further strength in crude or diesel would add weight to the case for moving sooner. Next week’s Fed commentary, before the pre-meeting blackout, is the next test of whether officials push back on October pricing.

---

One Fed president is hearing about prices everywhere he goes, and the Fed’s own survey says businesses are hearing about diesel even more.

Summary:

Two Federal Reserve releases on Wednesday painted a picture of inflation pressure that is broadening rather than fading, hours after US consumer price data came in hotter than expected. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee described the September figures as discouraging, and the Fed’s Beige Book survey showed price growth intensifying in parts of the country, driven increasingly by diesel costs.

Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, well above the Fed’s 2% target and ahead of economists’ forecasts. Higher gasoline costs linked to the Iran war accounted for much of the strength, while rising software and toy prices pointed to AI-driven demand and tariffs.

Speaking to Yahoo Finance, Goolsbee said he was concerned not only with the headline number but with the detail. Services inflation, he said, showed little sign of improvement and ran above 5% in the latest reading, a component that cannot be explained by tariffs or oil prices. He said that everywhere he went in the Midwest, he heard about costs and prices but very little that suggested a downturn or recession risk. In his view, that makes demand-side overheating a greater worry than a straightforward supply shock.

Goolsbee did not say how he thought the Fed should respond in the near term. However, he said there was no ambiguity about the central bank’s job if inflation stays high: it must prevent overheating from building, because demand-driven inflation tends to be persistent and hard to reverse. He said the Fed would get inflation back to 2%.

The Beige Book, which compiles business commentary from the Fed’s 12 regional banks, reinforced those concerns. Three districts described price growth as robust and eight as moderate, with three of those eight saying it was intensifying. Diesel fuel costs were cited 21 times, compared with two in the previous report and none in the surveys taken just before the US-Israeli war with Iran began in late February. Dallas Fed contacts named diesel as the most common factor pushing up costs, affecting freight, agriculture and airfares, and squeezing margins across many industries. Contacts also pointed to pressure from other commodities, tariffs and insurance.

The labour market remained stuck in a low-hire, low-fire pattern. Several districts noted the absence of mass layoffs, but five said firms were cutting staff by not replacing departing workers or by delaying hiring. Several also reported cost-of-living pressure feeding into wage demands. Artificial intelligence featured too: one business services firm told the Chicago Fed that AI productivity gains had allowed it to reduce headcount through attrition.

Housing was a clear weak spot. Mortgage rates rising toward three-year highs pushed buyers out of the market and kept existing owners from moving. Trade tensions with Canada were cited as a drag on manufacturing and tourism in four districts. The survey data were collected on or before October 5.

The Fed raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4% in September and signalled one more increase this year. Key officials have played down a move at the October 27-28 meeting, pointing instead toward December, but markets are now pricing close to a 40% chance of a hike this month.

titre: Fed's Beige Book:  Nine of 12 districts report growth as price pressures broaden
titre_fr: Fed's Beige Book:  Nine of 12 districts report growth as price pressures broaden
contenu:
The October Beige Book shows an economy losing a step while inflation pressures intensify. The national summary dropped its headline characterization of activity entirely. August said activity “increased modestly”; this report simply tallies the districts and notes that reports outside of manufacturing “indicate little growth overall.” Philadelphia and New York both slowed to slight growth from modest, while Chicago slipped to flat. Manufacturing is doing the heavy lifting, led by a sharp pickup in Dallas along with continued strength in data centers, power generation and defense.

The consumer has stalled. August described spending as growing slightly; now most districts report little or no change, and more than half said spending was being driven by high-income households. The strain is spreading up the income ladder. San Francisco said pressure on lower-income families has spread to middle-income households, and New York noted rising 401(k) hardship withdrawals and earned-wage advances. In Cleveland, a record 87% of surveyed nonprofits said their clients’ finances deteriorated. Boston, Minneapolis and San Francisco all flagged a drop in Canadian tourists.

Prices are the biggest shift. In August, only one district reported robust price growth and only one said the pace had accelerated. Now it’s three and four, respectively. Higher oil prices showed up in every district report, with diesel the most commonly cited cost. The forward-looking language is more concerning for the Fed: firms expect further increases as hedges and fixed contracts expire and get repriced. Philadelphia’s future prices indexes are among the highest readings in 35 years, and a New York food manufacturer said it hadn’t seen such broad-based pressures since the pandemic. Consumer-facing firms still can’t pass costs through, so margins are getting squeezed.

Hiring was marginally better than August, but real wages are a growing issue. Boston staffing contacts said raises are lagging inflation, and cost-of-living demands came up in several districts. AI also featured more prominently, with five districts reporting firms trimming staff through attrition, delaying hiring or planning fewer new jobs.

Higher rates are a new theme. Rising mortgage rates slowed housing further in Philadelphia, Kansas City said CRE loan spreads rose substantially, and Dallas bankers turned pessimistic, citing the Mideast conflict, inflation and the increase in the fed funds rate.

The FOMC meets Oct. 27-28 and along withtoday's CPI report, this adds to the case for hiking rates. We will hear from Chair Warsh late tomorrow.

titre: Today's Federal Reserve speaker slate suddenly got much more interesting
titre_fr: Today's Federal Reserve speaker slate suddenly got much more interesting
contenu:
The stakes around the October Federal Reserve meeting suddenly got much higher.

Today's US CPI report was hot across the board, including in core measures that are less volatile than the energy-driven headline. The bond market quickly repriced on the data, with US 2-year yields now up 15 basis points on the day to 4.94%.

In the Fed funds futures market, pricing is now right at 50/50 for a hike or hold this month. It's also critical to note that the Fed goes into the blackout period on Saturday.

That leaves just three days to shape the narrative if the Fed doesn't want to go into the meeting with raised stakes. That starts today with a 1:30 pm ET speech from Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin. I'm a fan of Barkin's level-headed style and he usually represents the core views of the Fed, so that's one to watch especially closely. That said, we just heard from Barkin this week and he didn't offer much in the way of guidance.

One notable recent comment from him was in late September when he said that this cycle could be like the 1990s mid-cycle adjustment. Barkin was comparing now to an easing cycle in the 1990s, when Greenspan cut rates by 75 bps over seven months at the end of 1995. So by that analogue -- if you took it directly -- would be more dovish than what is priced in now. He also said he would not yet make an overheating case, but economy is firming and not weakening and that businesses feel they have pricing power.

I would not put it past him to tip towards the hawkish side but he's usually not the guy to make the first big wave.

Next on the calendar will be Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who will appear on Yahoo Finance at 3 pm ET. He's candid but we have heard from him plenty and he has been leaning hawkish for awhile. That said, he hasn't been kicking down the door calling for rate hikes so if we see an incremental move in that direction today, it could be telling.

Tomorrow, we get to hear from the top guy with an 11:30 pm ET 'fireside chat' including Warsh at the IMF meetings. We will see if he sticks to his plan of not giving guidance or lets it out, my guess is that he will have to give a nod in one direction. Earlier that day, we will also hear from Hammack, who has been increasingly hawkish.

The Friday calendar is currently bare of Fed speakers but we will monitor that for any changes.

In terms of economic data, we also get PPI and retail sales tomorrow so those will be key.

titre: Lagarde: no second-round effects yet, but ECB can’t wait until they are in full view
titre_fr: Lagarde: no second-round effects yet, but ECB can’t wait until they are in full view
contenu:
Lagarde’s message leans hawkish at the margin. A central bank that will act on early hints, without waiting for clear evidence of second-round effects, could move sooner than markets expect if wage settlements firm. That supports front-end European yields and the euro on a relative basis. Energy is the key transmission channel. With inflation driven mainly by energy prices, a further jump in oil or gas from Gulf escalation would raise the odds of pre-emptive tightening, making crude and TTF gas direct inputs into ECB pricing. Her comments on France offer no backstop signal, so the French-German yield spread remains exposed to Paris’s budget politics.

-

Lagarde sees no wage-price spiral yet, but she has made clear the ECB will act on the first signs rather than wait for proof.

Summary:

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said the euro area has yet to see second-round effects from higher energy prices, but signalled the central bank would not wait for them to become fully visible before responding.

Lagarde said inflation has been rising predominantly, though not exclusively, as a result of energy prices. While there is no sign yet of those increases feeding through into broader wages and prices, she said policymakers must anticipate and look for early hints. The ECB is paying particular attention to collective bargaining arrangements, where expectations of future wage increases tend to show up first.

Second-round effects occur when an initial price shock, such as a jump in energy costs, prompts workers to seek higher wages and companies to raise prices further, turning a temporary spike into more persistent inflation. Lagarde’s emphasis on acting before those effects are fully evident suggests a readiness to respond pre-emptively if wage settlements begin to firm.

On the economy, Lagarde said growth is not brilliant, but that euro area growth of 1.1% in 2026 is not bad.

Asked about France’s debt, she said the primary and first solution lies in French fiscal policy. The remark puts the onus on Paris rather than the ECB as French borrowing costs face pressure. Goldman Sachs noted in a recent client discussion that the spread between French and German government bond yields has widened sharply amid political tensions over the French budget, an issue it expects to persist ahead of the French presidential election in the first half of next year.

Lagarde, who is French, also said she will not run for president of France.

Her comments leave energy prices and wage negotiations as the key indicators for the ECB’s next steps. A renewed rise in energy costs, or early evidence of stronger pay demands, would increase pressure on policymakers to act before inflation becomes entrenched.

European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said the euro area has yet to see second-round effects from higher energy prices, but signalled the central bank would not wait for them to become fully visible before responding.

Lagarde said inflation has been rising predominantly, though not exclusively, as a result of energy prices. While there is no sign yet of those increases feeding through into broader wages and prices, she said policymakers must anticipate and look for early hints. The ECB is paying particular attention to collective bargaining arrangements, where expectations of future wage increases tend to show up first.

Second-round effects occur when an initial price shock, such as a jump in energy costs, prompts workers to seek higher wages and companies to raise prices further, turning a temporary spike into more persistent inflation. Lagarde’s emphasis on acting before those effects are fully evident suggests a readiness to respond pre-emptively if wage settlements begin to firm.

On the economy, Lagarde said growth is not brilliant, but that euro area growth of 1.1% in 2026 is not bad.

Asked about France’s debt, she said the primary and first solution lies in French fiscal policy. The remark puts the onus on Paris rather than the ECB as French borrowing costs face pressure. Goldman Sachs noted in a recent client discussion that the spread between French and German government bond yields has widened sharply amid political tensions over the French budget, an issue it expects to persist ahead of the French presidential election in the first half of next year.

Lagarde, who is French, also said she will not run for president of France.

Her comments leave energy prices and wage negotiations as the key indicators for the ECB’s next steps. A renewed rise in energy costs, or early evidence of stronger pay demands, would increase pressure on policymakers to act before inflation becomes entrenched.

titre: Goldman Sachs says RBA minutes lower bar for November hike, with three hawkish signals
titre_fr: Goldman Sachs says RBA minutes lower bar for November hike, with three hawkish signals
contenu:
Goldman’s read raises the risk that the next RBA move comes sooner than its own base case. That leaves the third-quarter CPI release as the main event for the Australian dollar and short-dated bond yields. The minutes’ emphasis on domestic capacity shifts the focus from energy pass-through to underlying inflation, so even a moderate headline print could carry hawkish weight if services and core measures stay firm. Oil still matters at the margin: the minutes noted that domestic fuel prices were running well above the RBA’s August assumptions, and a renewed jump in crude tied to the Iran war would strengthen the case for tightening. Market pricing had already leaned toward further hikes before the September decision, so a hot CPI reading could quickly firm up expectations for November.

---

Goldman isn’t calling a November hike yet, but it thinks theRBA minuteshave opened the door, and the CPI report later this month will decide whether the board walks through it.

Summary:

Minutes of the Reserve Bank of Australia’s September policy meeting have likely lowered the bar for another interest rate increase in November, according to Goldman Sachs economists. The bank still expects rates to stay on hold.

In a report, three members of Goldman’s economics research team said they viewed the minutes, released on Tuesday, as more hawkish than Governor Michele Bullock’s press conference after the decision, for three reasons. Among them, the economists said the minutes showed increased concern about domestic capacity pressures, with the board treating July’s stronger-than-expected inflation data as evidence of that.

Goldman continues to expect the RBA to hold the cash rate at 4.60% at its next meeting. However, it judged that the minutes have lowered the threshold for a further hike in November, depending on the outcome of the third-quarter consumer price index report.

The minutes support that reading. They showed the board unanimously raised rates by 25 basis points at the 28 to 29 September meeting because several upside risks to inflation flagged in August had either materialised or were building. Those risks included a broader Middle East conflict pushing oil prices higher, cost pressures from the global AI boom, and tighter domestic capacity than assumed. Members said excess demand in the economy appeared greater than previously assessed. Staff increasingly questioned whether the unemployment rate consistent with target inflation was higher than thought, and business surveys pointed to a drift higher in firms’ inflation expectations.

The board also noted that, if global neutral interest rates have risen, the previous 4.35% cash rate was less restrictive than it had been two years earlier. It said holding steady while other central banks tightened could loosen Australian financial conditions through a weaker currency. Members concluded that they would remain attentive to incoming data and would raise rates further if required.

The third-quarter CPI report, due on 28 October at 00:30 GMT (20:30 ET on 27 October), now looks pivotal. The RBA’s next decision follows on 3 November at 03:30 GMT (22:30 ET on 2 November), alongside its updated quarterly forecasts. A strong reading on underlying and services inflation would test Goldman’s hold call and could push the board toward a second consecutive increase.

---

titre: Singapore: MAS could tighten again in 2027 if inflation risks materialise, says ANZ
titre_fr: Singapore: MAS could tighten again in 2027 if inflation risks materialise, says ANZ
contenu:
ANZ’s view tempers any dovish reading of Wednesday’s surprise hold. If markets come to see it as a pause within a tightening cycle, any Singapore dollar weakness against its trading partners could prove limited. The bar for a further move now appears to be evidence that inflation risks are materialising, which puts imported energy costs at the centre of the outlook. A renewed surge in oil or refined product prices tied to Gulf escalation would be the most likely trigger for MAS to steepen the slope of its policy band again. Easing in crude would strengthen the case for an extended hold.

--

ANZ reads the MAS hold as a breather, not a turning point: the earlier tightenings need time to work, but the door to more remains open.

Summary:

The Monetary Authority of Singapore could resume tightening next year if upside risks to inflation materialise, according to ANZ, one of the few forecasters that correctly predicted the central bank would leave policy unchanged on Wednesday.

Khoon Goh, head of Asia research at ANZ, said MAS judged there was no need to tighten further at this stage because the effects of its two earlier tightening moves, in April and July, are still feeding through the economy. Monetary policy works with a lag, and changes to the path of the Singapore dollar take time to show up in import prices and, in turn, consumer inflation.

That was despite a stronger economic backdrop than expected. Goh noted that third-quarter GDP growth beat expectations and that MAS still expects core inflation to remain slightly elevated in the near term. He stressed, however, that the decision does not signal the end of the tightening cycle, and that MAS could tighten again if upside inflation risks emerge next year.

ANZ’s call set it apart from the consensus. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters ahead of the decision had expected a tightening, making [Wednesday’s hold] a surprise to most of the market.

MAS, whichmanages policy through the Singapore dollar’s trade-weighted exchange rate, kept the rate of appreciation, width and centre of its policy band unchanged. Because the band remains on an appreciating path, the decision leaves the existing tightening stance in place without adding to it. [Our explainer on how MAS policy works] sets out how the three levers operate.

In its statement, the central bank said the economy should expand at a firm pace in the coming quarters before moderating as the AI cycle eases and global financial conditions tighten. It forecast core inflation to average 1.5% to 2.0% in 2026 and to ease more discernibly from mid-2027, but said risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside, including from a sharp and sustained rise in energy or food prices.

ANZ’s assessment suggests the next move, if any, is more likely to be a tightening than an easing. The path of imported costs, particularly energy, and whether core inflation proves stickier than MAS expects will shape the outlook for its upcoming reviews.

titre: How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers
titre_fr: How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers
contenu:
How Singapore’s monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers

Most central banks fight inflation by raising or cutting interest rates. Singapore does it differently. The Monetary Authority of Singapore steers the economy by managing the value of the Singapore dollar against a basket of its trading partners’ currencies. When MAS “tightens,” it lets the currency strengthen faster, which makes imports cheaper and cools inflation. When it “eases,” it slows or reverses that appreciation.

That is whyWednesday’s decision to hold policy steadywas framed entirely in terms of an exchange rate band, with no mention of an interest rate.

Why Singapore uses the exchange rate

Singapore is one of the most open economies in the world. It imports most of what it consumes, from food and fuel to raw materials, and trade flows are large relative to the size of its economy. That makes the exchange rate a far more powerful influence on prices than domestic interest rates.

There is also a practical constraint. Singapore allows capital to move freely in and out of the country. A central bank with open capital flows can control either its exchange rate or its interest rates, but not both. MAS chose the exchange rate in 1981, and local interest rates largely follow global rates, particularly those in the US.

What is the S$NEER?

The S$NEER, or Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate, measures the Singapore dollar against a weighted basket of the currencies of Singapore's main trading partners. MAS does not publish the basket's composition or weights. It manages the S$NEER within a policy band, stepping into the currency market when needed to keep it there.

The three levers

MAS adjusts policy through three features of the band, none of which it discloses precisely.

Analysts estimate the band’s width and slope from the currency’s movements, but MAS keeps the exact parameters private. That gives it room to act without inviting speculation against fixed levels.

How often MAS decides

MAS reviews policy four times a year, in January, April, July and October, having moved from a twice-yearly schedule in 2024. Decisions are released early in the Singapore morning, which is around midnight GMT.

The inflation measure that matters

MAS focuses on core inflation, which excludes accommodation and private transport costs. Those categories are heavily influenced by government policy and housing and car-ownership cycles, so stripping them out gives a cleaner read on underlying price pressures. On Wednesday, MAS forecast core inflation to average 1.5% to 2.0% for 2026 and to ease more discernibly from mid-2027.

What Wednesday’s decision means

By leaving all three levers unchanged, MAS kept the Singapore dollar on its existing appreciating path. That is still a restraint on imported inflation, just not an increased one. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected a tightening, most likely through a steeper slope, so the hold was a dovish surprise relative to expectations, even though the policy setting itself remains a tightening bias.

Key takeaway for traders

When reading an MAS statement, watch for the words “slope,” “width” and “centre.” Any change to them is the policy decision. For the Singapore dollar, the slope sets the medium-term direction against the basket, while a re-centring can produce a sharp immediate move. Because Singapore’s inflation is so sensitive to import costs, especially energy, oil prices are often a better guide to the next MAS move than local interest rates.

titre: Singapore’s MAS holds policy steady, surprising all 10 analysts who expected tightening
titre_fr: Singapore’s MAS holds policy steady, surprising all 10 analysts who expected tightening
contenu:
The decision is a dovish surprise against a unanimous call for tightening, which leaves the Singapore dollar vulnerable to some softening against its trading partners as positions built for a hawkish move unwind. The policy band still has an appreciating slope, though, so this is a pause in tightening, not an easing. Energy is the key swing factor. MAS explicitly flagged a sharp, sustained surge in energy prices as an upside risk, so a renewed jump in crude tied to Gulf escalation would put tightening firmly back on the table at the next review. Singapore’s position as a regional oil-trading and refining hub makes its imported inflation particularly sensitive to oil and refined product prices.

--

MAS chose patience over pre-emption, betting that slightly elevated inflation will ease on its own as the AI boom cools and import costs fade.

Summary:

The Monetary Authority of Singapore kept its monetary policy settings unchanged on Wednesday, defying expectations for a tightening as it judged that slightly elevated inflation should ease over time.

The central bank, which manages policy through the exchange rate, said it would maintain the current rate of appreciation of its policy band, known as the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate or S$NEER. There will be no change to the width of the band or the level at which it is centred. The band is already on an appreciating path, which helps restrain imported inflation, so the decision leaves that tightening bias in place without adding to it. All 10 analysts polled by Reuters had expected MAS to tighten.

MAS said the economy should continue to expand at a firm pace in the immediate quarters ahead, but moderate thereafter as the AI cycle eases from its exceptional pace and global financial conditions tighten. It expects AI-related activity to slow in the second half of 2027 and the economy’s positive output gap, a sign that demand is running ahead of capacity, to narrow through next year. The government will announce its growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 in November.

On prices, MAS expects firming imported cost pressures to keep both core and headline inflation at their current slightly elevated levels in the months ahead. Core inflation is forecast to average 1.5% to 2.0% for 2026 as a whole, before easing more discernibly from the middle of next year as import costs ebb.

The central bank stressed that significant uncertainty surrounds the outlook and that, for now, risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. A sharp and sustained surge in global energy or food prices could lift Singapore’s import costs by more than forecast. On the other hand, a larger-than-expected rise in interest rates or a sharper pullback in AI-related investment could drag on growth and, in turn, inflation.

The hold suggests MAS is prepared to look through near-term price pressures on the view that they will fade, while keeping its appreciating policy stance in place. With risks still skewed to the upside, the path of energy prices and the strength of the AI cycle are likely to shape whether it moves at its next review.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore is the coutnry's central bank.

---

The hold suggests MAS is prepared to look through near-term price pressures on the view that they will fade, while keeping its appreciating policy stance in place. With risks still skewed to the upside, the path of energy prices and the strength of the AI cycle are likely to shape whether it moves at its next review.

titre: ICYMI - Three Fed officials signal inflation fight continues; Williams sees no 2027 hike
titre_fr: ICYMI - Three Fed officials signal inflation fight continues; Williams sees no 2027 hike
contenu:
With October largely priced out, Tuesday’s trio keeps December in focus for the next move.Williams’ commentson 2027 cap how far markets can push expectations for the peak rate. That should limit the upside for longer-dated Treasury yields and the dollar unless the data turns. Barkin’s warning that shocks are continuing gives the hawkish camp an opening if inflation stays sticky. Oil is the swing factor. Williams’ benign outlook assumes energy won’t add to inflation next year, so a renewed crude surge, for example from escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi energy sites, would undercut that view and strengthen the case for more tightening. For now, oil is effectively a direct input into Fed pricing.

---Three Fed voices agree the inflation fight isn’t over; the open question is whether today’s shocks fade on their own or keep the Fed hiking into 2027.

Summary:

Three Federal Reserve officials on Tuesday signalled that the fight against inflation is not over, with two backing one more interest rate increase this year, though New York Fed President John Williams suggested the tightening cycle may end there.

Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin, speaking at Howard University, said the Fed’s 2% inflation target is not out of reach and can be achieved. He said it is clear that inflation is proving enduring and that shocks to prices are continuing, making it sensible for the Fed to act. Barkin, who does not vote on policy this year, also said policymakers can see the effect of artificial intelligence investment on US inflation.

Williams, who is vice chair of the Fed’s rate-setting committee, told Bloomberg News he had not changed his view that one more rate hike may be appropriate in 2026. He said he currently sees no reason to believe the Fed would need to do more in 2027, though the outlook could change and policymakers must keep watching the data. Williams expects inflation to fall substantially next year to near 2% for 2027 as a whole, as tariff effects fade completely and energy prices stop adding to inflation. He acknowledged that high energy prices tied to the Middle East war and tech-related investment are lifting near-term pressures, but argued the economy is not overheating.

Boston Fed President Susan Collins struck a firmer tone. In prepared remarks, [she said she expects the Fed to raise rates a bit further before the end of the year] and described the risk of high inflation as elevated and the central bank’s main focus. She expects headline and core inflation to run above target in coming months because of higher prices for diesel, jet fuel and heating oil. In [follow-up comments, Collins said economic uncertainty is elevated] and that she is watching how broad-based inflation pressures are.

Together, the comments point to a Fed that agrees on the near-term direction but is split on the nature of the problem. Williams sees inflation driven by specific shocks that should fade, while Barkin’s emphasis on continuing shocks and Collins’ focus on the breadth of price pressures point to a risk that inflation proves more persistent.

The Fed raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% in September. Williams’ comments late that month led markets to largely price out a hike at the October 27-28 meeting, leaving December as the more likely timing for the next move.

titre: Fed’s Collins says uncertainty is elevated as she watches breadth of inflation pressures
titre_fr: Fed’s Collins says uncertainty is elevated as she watches breadth of inflation pressures
contenu:
Collins’ focus on how widespread inflation is moves attention to core and services prices, not just the headline energy-driven numbers. Signs of fuel costs spreading into broader prices would firm December hike pricing and support front-end yields and the dollar. For oil, that means sustained strength in crude and products now carries a second-round risk the Fed is explicitly watching. Her stress on elevated uncertainty also leaves room for the data to delay the next move, which caps how aggressively markets can price an October hike.

---

Collins has already called for another hike, and now she is spelling out what will set the timing: whether inflation spreads beyond energy in an uncertain economy.

Summary:

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Tuesday that economic uncertainty is elevated and that she is paying close attention to how broad-based inflation pressures are, as she set out the factors that will shape her view on the timing of the next rate move.

Collins said she is very focused on the inflation data and that she looks at the economy holistically when weighing the future path of policy. Her emphasis on breadth suggests she will be watching whether price pressures spread into a wider range of goods and services, rather than staying concentrated in a few categories.

The comments add detailto remarks earlier in the dayin which [Collins said she expects the Fed to raise rates again before the end of 2026]. In that speech text, prepared for a banking conference at the Boston Fed, she said she had supported the central bank’s quarter-point hike in September, which took the policy rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, and called the risk of high inflation the Fed’s main focus.

Collins has flagged several forces that could keep inflation above the Fed’s 2% target, including investment in data centres and artificial intelligence infrastructure, the ongoing effect of tariffs, and energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. She has said she expects both headline and core inflation to run above target in coming months, citing recent increases in prices for refined fuels such as diesel, jet fuel and heating oil.

Her baseline outlook remains constructive, with healthy growth, a job market near full employment and a gradual return of inflation to target. Her latest comments make clear, however, that she sees the outlook as uncertain and that the incoming data will decide how quickly she wants policy to move.

Policymaker projections released in September pointed to one more increase this year. Several Fed officials have suggested in recent weeks that it is more likely in December than at the October 27-28 meeting, and Collins has said the policy path into the new year will depend on the data.

titre: Fed’s Collins backs another rate hike by year-end, flags three inflation pressures
titre_fr: Fed’s Collins backs another rate hike by year-end, flags three inflation pressures
contenu:
Collins’ remarks reinforce expectations of another quarter-point rise before year-end, with recent Fed commentary leaning towards December rather than this month’s meeting. That should keep front-end Treasury yields supported and limit room for a sustained dollar pullback while hikes stay in play. For oil traders, the significance is the feedback loop: further gains in crude and refined products tied to the Middle East war now feed straight into Fed hike expectations, so energy strength carries rates and dollar consequences. A softer run of data would be the main thing to cool that pricing.

---

Earlier:

---

Collins sees a resilient economy as giving the Fed licence to keep tightening, with war-driven fuel costs the clearest reason inflation won’t get back to target on its own.

Summary:

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins said on Tuesday she expects the US central bank will need to lift interest rates again before the end of 2026, arguing that further tightening is needed to return inflation to the Fed’s 2% target in a timely and lasting way.

In prepared remarks for a banking conference at the Boston Fed, reported by Reuters, Collins said she had supported the Federal Open Market Committee’s decision last month to raise its policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. She indicated that a modest additional increase would likely be appropriate this year, while stressing that her view on both the need for and timing of further action would rest on the full body of incoming data and how it shapes the balance of risks.

Collins framed the inflation fight as the Fed’s central task. With growth holding up and the labour market broadly balanced, she said policymakers have room to concentrate on bringing inflation back to target, a goal the Fed has now missed for more than five years. She described the risk of persistently high inflation as elevated and the central bank’s main focus at present.

Her baseline outlook was largely constructive. In what she called the most likely scenario, the economy keeps growing at a healthy pace, the job market stays close to full employment and inflation eases gradually back to 2%, helped by ongoing efficiency gains that keep supply and demand in balance. She added that a stable labour market should continue to underpin consumer spending.

Collins nonetheless identified three forces that could complicate that path: heavy investment in data centres and other artificial intelligence infrastructure, the continuing effect of tariffs, and higher energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. She said she expects both headline and core inflation to run above target again in the coming months, pointing to the recent jump in prices for refined products such as jet fuel, diesel and heating oil.

Projections published at the September meeting already pencilled in another increase before year-end. Several Fed officials have signalled in recent weeks that the move is more likely to come in December than at the October 27-28 meeting, and Collins’ comments keep a further hike firmly on the table while leaving its timing open. She said the policy path into the new year would depend on the data.

titre: BoE’s Greene warns waiting for second-round inflation effects would be too late
titre_fr: BoE’s Greene warns waiting for second-round inflation effects would be too late
contenu:
Greene’s remarks reinforce the hawkish wing of the MPC and support market expectations of a November hike, which recent reports put at around 84%. Her warning about second-round effects ties directly to the energy shock from the Iran war: if higher oil and diesel costs feed into wages and pricing, the case for tightening strengthens further, keeping short-dated gilt yields and sterling sensitive to energy prices. The comments also add pressure on the gilt market at a time when global bond yields are already elevated. Upcoming UK wage and inflation data will be key for whether her view gains wider support on the committee.

--Greene’s message is simple: by the time inflation shows up in wages and prices, it will be too late, so the Bank should move before it gets there.

Summary:

Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene said UK monetary policy is not that restrictive, warning that waiting for second-round inflation effects to become visible before acting would leave the central bank responding too late.

Greene, an external member of the Monetary Policy Committee, said she sees the bigger risk as failing to be proactive enough in tackling inflation, rather than raising interest rates too soon. Second-round effects occur when an initial price shock, such as a rise in energy costs, feeds into wages and broader price-setting, making inflation more persistent.

Her comments reinforce her position as one of the more hawkish members of the committee. Greene voted for a quarter-point rate increase at the Bank’s July and September meetings, when she was among three members outvoted by a majority that preferred to keep rates on hold.

Greene has made similar arguments in recent days. Last week, she said she expected the UK to see some second-round effects from the current inflation cycle and voiced concern that wage growth of around 3.5% next year would be worrying, raising the risk that higher prices feed into pay deals and prompt firms to raise prices further.

She said the International Monetary Fund’s latest forecasts for the UK did not surprise her. The IMF raised its 2026 UK growth forecast to 1.3% this week, citing stronger AI-related investment, while warning that the global outlook faces significant risks from the war in the Middle East and elevated energy prices.

The UK, like other major economies, is grappling with inflation pressure from higher oil and diesel prices following the conflict involving Iran. Policymakers who favour acting early argue that letting those costs become embedded in wages and inflation expectations would ultimately require more painful tightening later.

Markets have increasingly priced a rate hike at the Bank’s November meeting, and Greene’s remarks suggest she will continue to make the case for tighter policy. The next round of UK wage and inflation data will help determine whether that view gains broader support on the committee.

titre: RBA minutes show three reasons for hike to 4.60% and leave door open to further increases
titre_fr: RBA minutes show three reasons for hike to 4.60% and leave door open to further increases
contenu:
The minutes read hawkish,not unexpectedly,with the board explicitly keeping further hikes on the table and markets already pricing roughly another 15 basis points by year-end and 30 basis points in the first half of 2027. Oil is central to the outlook: domestic fuel prices were running well above the RBA’s August assumptions, and any further escalation of the Iran war would feed directly into the risk of more tightening. The board’s concern that a lagging RBA could weaken the Australian dollar suggests it is willing to keep pace with other central banks, which should support the currency against a backdrop of rising global yields. Rate-sensitive sectors such as banks, property and consumer discretionary remain vulnerable, given falling house prices and the board’s view that household spending must stay subdued for some time.

---

The RBA has concluded the economy is running hotter and the neutral rate is higher than it thought, which is central bank language for “we may not be done yet”.

Summary:

The Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates last month because several of the upside risks to inflation it had flagged in August had either materialised or were building, according to minutes of the 28 to 29 September meeting released on Tuesday. The board signalled it was prepared to tighten further if needed.

The board voted unanimously to lift the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60%. Members said the August forecasts, which had inflation returning to the midpoint of the target range by around late 2027, depended on a series of favourable developments that no longer looked likely to all occur.

The minutes set out three main arguments for the move. First, the risks identified in August had largely come to pass. The Middle East conflict had broadened and oil prices were well above the level assumed in the forecasts, with domestic petrol and diesel prices running about 13% higher than projected. Global cost pressures were intensifying, driven partly by extraordinary demand for AI-related products, and domestic capacity appeared tighter than assessed. Second, members judged that responding quickly would best balance their inflation and employment goals, given inflation has been above target for an extended period and surveys point to a risk that business inflation expectations are rising. Third, the board said the cash rate might not be high enough to restore balance within a reasonable timeframe even if the risks did not fully materialise.

That last point reflected a significant shift in thinking about the neutral interest rate, the level at which policy neither stimulates nor restrains the economy. Members said that if market signals of a higher global neutral rate were correct, the previous 4.35% cash rate was less restrictive than it had been two years earlier. They added that if the RBA held still while other central banks tightened, Australian financial conditions could loosen through a weaker currency.

On the economy, the board noted June quarter growth was a little stronger than expected, driven by business investment that rose more than 10% over the year, partly reflecting data centre and renewable energy construction. Household consumption slowed to a below-trend pace, house prices fell faster than expected, and unemployment rose to 4.6% in August. Staff increasingly questioned whether the unemployment rate consistent with target inflation is higher than previously thought, which would mean more pressure on capacity than estimated. Unit labour cost growth, driven by weak productivity rather than strong wages, also remained above levels consistent with the target.
